title: Lesson 70: The Architecture Spectrum: Orchestration vs Autonomy
description: The spectrum between orchestration and autonomy: what each pole means, who owns the decision of what happens next, when to choose a workflow versus an agent, and how to hybridize a task so the deterministic parts stay deterministic and only the open-ended part gets agency.

questions.question: What distinguishes a workflow from an agent in how an agentic system is built?
options: A workflow fixes the path in code, while an agent lets the model choose its steps.
A workflow runs on a stronger underlying model, while an agent must use a weaker one.
A workflow never calls any tools, while an agent always calls at least one tool.
A workflow always runs locally, while an agent must always run in the cloud.
questions.explanation: The difference is not model capability but who owns the decision of what happens next. In a workflow the code fixes the path; in an agent the model dynamically directs its own process and tool use.

questions.question: Which task is the right fit for giving a model autonomy rather than fixing the path in code?
options: A task whose steps and branches can all be confidently written down well in advance.
A task where the route cannot be predicted and the goal is the contract.
A task where every input falls into one of a few known categories.
A task whose success can never be checked by any automated means.
questions.explanation: Autonomy earns its place only where orchestration cannot reach: open-ended work where the number of steps is hard to predict and you can trust the model within guardrails. If the steps or branches can be enumerated, a workflow is the more reliable, cheaper choice.

questions.question: Most of a system is predictable, but one step depends on free-form input the team cannot enumerate. What design fits?
options: Make the whole system one autonomous agent, since any open-ended part forces full autonomy.
Give the model autonomy over the predictable steps and fix only the free-form step in code.
Orchestrate the predictable steps and give only the free-form step a bounded agent.
Leave the system unbuilt, since one unpredictable step makes it unreliable.
questions.explanation: The through-line is to maximize determinism where the task allows it and spend autonomy only on the open-ended residue, bounded by a step cap, a small tool palette, and a check on its output. Production systems almost always land in the middle.
